newsitem.title: USA: Wife convicted of emigre husband's murder.
newsitem.headline: Wife convicted of emigre husband's murder.

text.p: A federal jury, after deliberating a day and a half, on Thursday convicted the estranged wife of a Soviet emigre of the axe murder of her husband.
Rita Gluzman, 49, was charged under a 1994 federal law making it a crime to cross state lines to abuse a spouse.
The law was intended to stop vengeful men from pursuing women, and she was the first woman to be charged under the federal statute.
Gluzman was stone-faced as the jury forewoman read the guilty verdict. Gluzman's mother, who was sitting in the second row of the spectator's section, sobbed softly.
The judge set sentencing for April 30, when she faces life in prison without parole.

The Gluzmans were embroiled in a bitter divorce after a 27-year marriage marked by forced separation, political exile and then professional success after leaving the Soviet Union in the late 1970s for Israel and then the United States.
Prosecutors said Gluzman killed her husband, Yakov Gluzman, 46, because he had filed for divorce and was planning to start a new life with another woman in Israel.
They said Gluzman travelled from her $540,000 Upper Saddle River, New Jersey, home to the Pearl River, New York, apartment of her estranged husband, a molecular biologist.

There, she and her cousin, Vladimir Zelenin. ambushed him with axes on April 6, prosecutors said. Zelenin pleaded guilty and testified against Gluzman in hopes of getting a reduced sentence. He has not yet been sentences.
According to trial testimony, the two cut their victim into more than 67 pieces.
Gluzman's defence attorneys argued Zelenin was solely responsible for the killing but that she was not involved.
One juror, who did not want to be identified, said he found Zelenin, the prosecution's main witness, highly credible.
"It was a combination of blows, the axes, what was used, that convinced us to convict," he said.
Zelenin was caught dumping 10 plastic garbage bags containing Gluzman's body parts into the Passaic River in New Jersey.
"I completed the killing of Yakov Gluzman together with Rita," he testified. "The idea of killing Yakov was the idea of Rita Gluzman."

Authorities opted to pursue federal charges against Gluzman rather than seek a state murder indictment because under New York law the testimony of an accomplice such as Zelenin cannot be used in obtaining a conviction. Under federal law, his testimony was admissible.
